analysis.one_liner: Ends tax breaks that reward US corporations for shifting profits and headquarters offshore.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee with 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise taxes on large US corporations that book profits in low-tax foreign countries, stripping out several tax breaks created by the 2017 tax law. It would also treat companies that moved their headquarters abroad on paper — but kept their executives and operations in the US — as American companies for tax purposes, and would close a special break for foreign oil and gas income. The bill never received a hearing or vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be ordinary taxpayers and domestically focused businesses. Multinational corporations would owe more tax on profits booked offshore, producing federal revenue that reduces pressure on other taxpayers or borrowing. Domestic-only companies would compete on a more level field, since rivals could no longer deduct income earned through foreign intangibles or shield foreign oil and gas income from US tax [S2] [S3]. Workers at US headquarters of "inverted" companies would also benefit, because the bill would tax corporations run from the US as US companies even if they reincorporated abroad [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the deductions that gave US multinationals reduced tax rates on foreign intangible income (FDII) and global intangible low-taxed income (GILTI), and eliminates the exemption for returns on tangible property held overseas, so more offshore profit is taxed in the US each year.
It ends the exclusion of foreign oil and gas extraction income from the offshore income subject to US tax, closing a carve-out for energy multinationals.

It tightens the rules on corporate inversions: a company would count as American for tax purposes if more than 50% of its stock is held by former US shareholders, or if its management and control stay in the US, rather than escaping US tax by reincorporating in a low-tax country.

It treats foreign corporations whose executive officers and senior management are primarily located in the US — including investment vehicles with $50 million or more in assets managed from the US — as domestic corporations, preventing companies from disappearing into foreign mailboxes while being run from America.
It limits the interest deduction that US members of large multinational reporting groups can claim, discouraging the practice of loading US entities with debt to shrink their taxable income.

analysis.who_pays: US-based multinational corporations — and their shareholders — would bear the cost through higher taxes on offshore profits, smaller interest deductions, and loss of benefits from inversion structures. Multinationals with foreign oil and gas income would lose a specific carve-out. Companies that had already inverted would face back-loaded US tax treatment. Business groups would argue some of the cost passes through to consumers or to investment in US operations [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Raising taxes only on US-based multinationals, while foreign competitors face no equivalent, could tilt investment and headquarters decisions toward other countries — the same concern the 2017 international provisions the bill repeals were meant to address.

The interest-deduction limit applies to any US corporation in a reporting group with over $100 million in gross receipts, which would raise the cost of borrowing for large companies that finance investment with debt, and disallowed interest could only be carried forward five years.

Treating foreign corporations managed from the US as domestic would sweep in foreign-owned investment funds and companies with US-based executives, which could deter foreign investment managers and multinational headquarters from locating in the United States.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real tax-avoidance channels — profit shifting, inversions, debt loading, and the foreign oil and gas carve-out — and the revenue would come from some of the most profitable companies in the world. But the design is one-sided: it raises taxes on US-headquartered multinationals without coordinating with other countries, so it could speed up exactly the offshoring of headquarters and investment it is meant to punish. The management-and-control provision is broad enough to catch foreign investment firms. It is a pro-revenue bill with real enforceability value, but also real risk of pushing corporate activity abroad rather than raising the revenue projected.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Whitehouse introduced the bill on March 13, 2019, with Senator Van Hollen joining, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
The bill had 2 cosponsors, both Democrats, and no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote — appears in its history for the rest of the Congress.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US multinational corporations that would have paid more tax under the bill are better off, as are companies using inversion and offshore-profit structures; the 2017 tax law's international provisions remain in place. The Senate Finance Committee majority, which never scheduled action, avoided a fight over the 2017 tax law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinationals that keep offshore tax breaks

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote; all of its support on record — the sponsor and 2 cosponsors — was Democratic, and no Republican backed it.

industries.note: The bill's core provisions would tax their offshore profits at full rates each year instead of allowing reduced-rate deductions and an exemption for returns on tangible assets held abroad, ending the incentive to book intangible profits in low-tax countries.
It repeals the exclusion of foreign oil and gas extraction income from the tested income of controlled foreign corporations, ending a carve-out that shields overseas extraction profits from US tax.

Companies that reincorporated abroad after December 2017 while keeping majority US ownership or US-based management would be taxed as domestic corporations, and foreign corporations run from the US would be pulled into the US tax net.
Firms without foreign operations would compete on more level terms once rivals lose deductions tied to shifting income and profits offshore.
